title: Paris, 1919: The Peace Conference and Those Outside the Door
subtitle: The Paris Peace Conference, Quai d'Orsay and Versailles, January–June 1919
intro: On 18 January 1919 delegates from some thirty states gathered at the French Foreign Ministry on the Quai d'Orsay to make the peace after the First World War. Within days the real work had passed to a Council of Ten, two leaders from each of the five great powers, and from late March to a Council of Four: Wilson, Lloyd George, Clemenceau and Orlando, meeting in Wilson's study with an interpreter and, later, one secretary. Everything else was outside the door.

This chapter lays the official record beside the private one. The minutes of the Council of Ten and the plenary sessions printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, and Paul Mantoux's interpreter's notes of the Four, give what was said in the room as secretaries summarised it. Around them stand the diaries and dated memoranda of those close to it: Colonel House, the sidelined Secretary of State Lansing, Wilson's doctor Grayson, Lloyd George's secretary Frances Stevenson, the young diplomat Harold Nicolson. Several eyes left no diary at all, only speeches, memoranda and petitions, and the form tags say so.

The room heard claims that could not all be satisfied. China and Japan both claimed the German rights in Shandong. The Emir Faisal asked independence for the Arab lands of Asia while France pointed to its wartime agreements and the Zionist delegation pressed its case for Palestine. Japan asked for a clause on racial equality, and won a majority that the chair ruled insufficient. Germany was summoned in May to receive the terms, not to negotiate them. The chapter reports what each side said and decided, with the evidence, and gives no verdicts.

Some of the most consequential people in Paris that year never got into the room. W. E. B. Du Bois convened a Pan-African Congress at the Grand Hôtel in February. A young Vietnamese who signed himself Nguyen Ai Quoc sent the delegations eight modest demands in June. In Beijing, on 4 May, students marched against the Shandong decision. Their papers sit in the American delegation's files, received and unanswered.

Most of the private sources here were first published after 1928 (Nicolson in 1933, Stevenson in 1971, Mantoux in 1955, Koo's oral history decades later), so they are summarised, not quoted. Short quotations come only from English texts published before 1929, chiefly Lansing's 1921 memoir, House's papers as printed in 1928 and The Crisis, and from US government records within twelve words.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. The Republic of China had adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1912; Japanese documents of the time also carry Taishō 8 era dating. The conference ran on Paris time, and news of its decisions reached Beijing and Tokyo by cable within a day or two. Several diaries were written up the morning after, and memoir recollections (Koo) are fixed to their dates only by the events they describe.

eyes.name: Thomas Woodrow Wilson
eyes.role: President of the United States, aged 62; head of the American delegation and chairman of the League of Nations Commission
eyes.where: His residence at 11 Place des États-Unis, the Quai d'Orsay and the Hôtel Crillon; home to Washington mid-February to mid-March
eyes.form: official minutes and records of his words (no diary)
eyes.authenticity: Wilson kept no diary in Paris. His words survive in the US secretaries' notes printed in Foreign Relations of the United States (FRUS), in Paul Mantoux's interpreter's notes of the Council of Four (published 1955), and in the Papers of Woodrow Wilson. Minutes are summaries in indirect speech, not transcripts.
eyes.bio: Wilson came to Paris to make a League of Nations part of the peace and spent six months bargaining for it. Seen through the minutes, he is the chairman who ruled the racial-equality amendment out, the arbiter of the Shandong settlement, and the man petitioners outside the door most hoped to reach.

sources.title: FRUS, Paris Peace Conference 1919, vol. III: Council of Ten, 6 Feb 1919
FRUS vol. III: Plenary session at the Trianon Palace, 7 May 1919

eyes.name: Edward Mandell House
eyes.role: 'Colonel' House, aged 60; Wilson's closest adviser and an American peace commissioner, member of the League Commission
eyes.where: Hôtel Crillon, Place de la Concorde
eyes.authenticity: House dictated a diary throughout the conference; the original is in the Edward M. House Papers at Yale. Charles Seymour printed extensive extracts in The Intimate Papers of Colonel House, vol. IV (1928), and Arthur Link reprinted the Paris entries in the Papers of Woodrow Wilson. House wrote with an eye on posterity and often placed himself at the centre.
eyes.bio: House ran the American delegation while Wilson was in Washington and negotiated compromises that Wilson, on his return, came to resent. The diary records a friendship cooling into silence; the two men never met again after June 1919.

sources.title: American Heritage: 'The End of a Friendship: Wilson and House'
American Heritage: 'Epilogue'

eyes.name: Robert Lansing
eyes.role: US Secretary of State, aged 54; nominally second in the American delegation
eyes.authenticity: Lansing wrote dated memoranda 'for his files' through the conference and printed many of them in The Peace Negotiations: A Personal Narrative (1921), written after Wilson dismissed him in February 1920. The book is a self-justification, but the memoranda carry their original dates.
eyes.bio: A lawyer who distrusted the Covenant and thought Wilson should not have come, Lansing sat in the Council of Ten and then watched the Council of Four from outside it. His notes are the American dissent from inside the delegation: on secrecy, on Shandong, and on the finished treaty.

sources.title: The Peace Negotiations: A Personal Narrative (1921), Project Gutenberg

eyes.name: Paul Mantoux
eyes.role: French historian, aged 41; official interpreter to the Council of Ten and the Council of Four
eyes.where: Quai d'Orsay; Wilson's study in the Place des États-Unis
eyes.authenticity: Mantoux took notes in order to interpret and later wrote them up; they were published as Les Délibérations du Conseil des Quatre (1955) and in English, edited by Arthur Link, in 1992. Maurice Hankey kept the official British minutes from 19 April, so the two records can be compared. Mantoux's notes are closer to direct speech but are still his reconstruction.
eyes.bio: For most of the spring only four statesmen, the British secretary Hankey and Mantoux sat in the room where the treaty was made. Because the Four shared no common language, Mantoux's notes are the nearest thing to a record of what they actually said to each other.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III: Council of Ten, 6 Feb 1919 (Mantoux listed as interpreter)

eyes.name: Harold George Nicolson
eyes.role: British Foreign Office official, aged 32; expert on Balkan and Greek questions on the territorial commissions
eyes.where: Hotel Majestic (British delegation) and Lloyd George's flat in the rue Nitot
eyes.vantage_label: junior diplomat at the table's edge
eyes.authenticity: Nicolson published his 1919 diary as the second half of Peacemaking 1919 (1933), with a long retrospective essay before it. He admitted to some trimming. As a post-1928 publication it is summarised here, never quoted.
eyes.bio: Nicolson drew frontiers for a living that spring and later wrote the best-known account of the conference's exhaustion and haste. His diary is the view of the clever, overworked expert who sees great decisions made in minutes.

sources.title: Peacemaking 1919 (catalogue record)
The Spectator, 16 June 1933: review 'Reflections on Peacemakers'

eyes.name: Frances Louise Stevenson
eyes.role: Lloyd George's private secretary and companion, aged 30 (later his second wife)
eyes.vantage_label: secretary in the Prime Minister's household
eyes.form: diary and letters to her family
eyes.authenticity: Her diary, found in the Beaverbrook Library, was edited by A. J. P. Taylor as Lloyd George: A Diary (1971). Her letters home from Paris are held by the National Library of Wales. Both are post-1928 publications and are summarised only.
eyes.bio: Stevenson saw Lloyd George at breakfast and late at night, between Council sessions. Her diary and letters show the British leader's moods and his doubts about the severity of the terms.

sources.title: National Library of Wales: Frances Stevenson's Versailles letters
NLW archive file H/9: letters from Versailles
The Diary Junction: Frances Stevenson

eyes.name: Cary Travers Grayson
eyes.role: Rear admiral and Wilson's personal physician, aged 40
eyes.authenticity: Grayson kept a daily diary in Paris; it is held by the Woodrow Wilson Presidential Library and printed in the Papers of Woodrow Wilson (vols. 54–61). He was protective of Wilson and his diary avoids clinical detail about the April illness.
eyes.bio: Grayson was with Wilson from breakfast to bedtime and travelled with him to Brest and back. His diary is the household view of the conference: the President's health, his temper and his routine.

sources.title: Cary T. Grayson Diary, Woodrow Wilson Presidential Library digital archive
Doughboy Foundation: 'Did Woodrow Wilson Have the Flu in Paris?'

eyes.name: Makino Nobuaki
eyes.role: Baron, former foreign minister, aged 57; de facto leader of the Japanese delegation and member of the League Commission
eyes.where: Hotel Bristol, rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré
eyes.vantage_label: great-power delegate outside the inner council
eyes.form: speeches and statements in the official record
eyes.authenticity: Makino's words survive in the FRUS minutes, in David Hunter Miller's record of the League Commission, and in the plenary protocols. These are other people's summaries of his speeches. His later memoir (Kaikoroku) was written decades afterwards.
eyes.bio: Makino sat on the Council of Ten but was rarely included when the Four met alone. He carried two claims: German rights in Shandong, and a clause on the equality of nations and their nationals. The record shows how differently the two were received.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III: Council of Ten, 28 Jan 1919
Racial Equality Proposal (encyclopedia overview)

eyes.name: V. K. Wellington Koo (Gu Weijun)
eyes.role: Chinese minister to Washington, aged 30; Columbia PhD; China's principal speaker at the conference
eyes.authenticity: His 28 January statement is in FRUS. His recollections come from the Columbia University Chinese Oral History Project, recorded in the 1960s and 1970s and published in Chinese as Gu Weijun huiyilu (13 vols, 1983–94). Entries drawn from that memoir were remembered fifty years later and are flagged accordingly.
eyes.bio: Koo made China's case for Shandong in polished English before the Council of Ten and won the room's sympathy, then watched the Four award the German rights to Japan. He was among the delegates who decided not to sign the treaty.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III: Council of Ten, 28 Jan 1919
Columbia Magazine: 'Columbia's Role in the Paris Peace Conference'

eyes.name: Faisal ibn al-Husayn
eyes.role: Emir, aged 33; son of Sharif Husayn of Mecca and delegate of the Kingdom of the Hijaz
eyes.where: Hôtel Continental, rue de Rivoli; London in January
eyes.authenticity: Faisal's memoranda of 1 and 29 January 1919 were submitted in English. The Council of Ten's minutes of 6 February summarise his oral statement in indirect speech. His agreement with Chaim Weizmann (3 January 1919) carries a reservation in Arabic in his own hand, translated by Lawrence. Each of these was shaped by translation.
eyes.bio: Faisal had led the Arab revolt's northern army and arrived in Paris to find the French expecting Syria under the 1916 Sykes–Picot understanding and the Zionists pressing their own claim to Palestine. His statements set out the Arab case in his own terms.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III: Council of Ten, 6 Feb 1919
Faisal–Weizmann correspondence, 1 Jan–3 Mar 1919 (documents)

eyes.name: Thomas Edward Lawrence
eyes.role: British army officer, aged 30; adviser and interpreter to Faisal
eyes.where: Hôtel Continental and the Quai d'Orsay
eyes.authenticity: Lawrence's letters were collected by David Garnett (1938) and Malcolm Brown (1988). His presence at the 6 February session is recorded in the FRUS minutes; the common story that he translated Faisal's Arabic speech comes from later accounts, not from the minutes.
eyes.bio: Lawrence attended the conference in British uniform and Arab headdress, working for Faisal while still a British officer. He was caught between his own government, the French and the promises he believed had been made to the Arabs.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III: Council of Ten, 6 Feb 1919 (Lawrence listed present)

eyes.name: William Edward Burghardt Du Bois
eyes.where: Grand Hôtel, boulevard des Capucines; office at the Hôtel de Malte
eyes.authenticity: Du Bois reported from Paris in The Crisis (March–May 1919) and in syndicated articles in Black newspapers. These are contemporary published writings, partisan in purpose, and may be quoted briefly because they predate 1929.
eyes.bio: Du Bois sailed to France in December 1918 to document the treatment of Black American troops and to put Africa's future before the conference. With Blaise Diagne, the Senegalese deputy, he convened a Pan-African Congress a few streets from the Quai d'Orsay.

sources.title: The Crisis, March 1919: Memorandum to M. Diagne and Others
World History Commons: Du Bois's newspaper report on the 1919 Pan-African Congress
Library of Congress: The Pan-African Conference

eyes.name: Nguyen Ai Quoc (later Ho Chi Minh)
eyes.role: Photo retoucher and political organiser, about 29; one of a group of Vietnamese patriots in Paris
eyes.vantage_label: petitioner who never reached the room
eyes.authenticity: The letter of 18 June 1919 to Lansing, with its enclosure 'Revendications du peuple annamite', is in the US National Archives (RG 256). The petition was drafted collectively, probably with Phan Chu Trinh and Phan Van Truong; the signature 'Nguyen Ai Quoc' was at first a group name before he made it his own.
eyes.bio: The young man who would lead Vietnam's independence struggle asked not for independence but for eight reforms within French rule. His petition went to every delegation; the American file shows it was received, filed and not acted on.

sources.title: DocsTeach (US National Archives): Letter from Ho Chi Minh to Secretary of State Robert Lansing
UMass Boston: text of the letter

eyes.name: Ulrich Graf von Brockdorff-Rantzau
eyes.role: German Foreign Minister, aged 49; head of the German peace delegation
eyes.where: Hôtel des Réservoirs, Versailles (delegation fenced in)
eyes.vantage_label: the defeated party, summoned to receive terms
eyes.authenticity: His 7 May speech is printed in English translation in the FRUS protocol of the session; the German text is in the Reichstag and Foreign Office records. The German notes of May–June were published by both sides. No private diary is used here.
eyes.bio: Brockdorff-Rantzau was not allowed to negotiate, only to receive terms and answer in writing. His speech at the Trianon Palace was the only time a German voice was heard in a full session before the signing, and he resigned rather than put his name to the treaty.

sources.title: FRUS vol. III: Plenary session at the Trianon Palace, 7 May 1919
The Spectator, 10 May 1919

entries.headline: Proposing a Pan-African Congress to Diagne
entries.digest: Du Bois drew up a memorandum for Blaise Diagne and others proposing a congress in Paris in February. It would gather reports on the condition of Black peoples everywhere and press the Peace Conference to give them a voice and protection in the League of Nations. The principles listed included land rights, education and gradual self-government. A later cable reported that the French government would permit the meeting.
entries.source_note: The Crisis 17:5 (March 1919), pp. 224–25, dated Paris, 1 January 1919.

entries.headline: Signing an agreement with Weizmann, with a condition
entries.digest: In London, Faisal signed an agreement with Chaim Weizmann on cooperation between Arabs and Jews in Palestine, encouraging Jewish immigration while protecting Arab peasants. In Arabic beneath the text he added that he would be bound only if the Arabs obtained the independence he had asked for; Lawrence translated the reservation. Both sides later read the agreement in their own way.
entries.source_note: Faisal–Weizmann agreement, 3 Jan 1919, with Faisal's Arabic reservation; correspondence collected on israeled.org.

entries.headline: No plan of work: 'We putter around'
entries.digest: Two days before the opening, Lansing complained in a note that the American commissioners had no programme because Wilson had turned down a skeleton treaty prepared for him. The delegation, he wrote, drifted without direction.
entries.quote: We putter around in an aimless sort of way and get nowhere.
entries.source_note: Lansing, The Peace Negotiations (1921), note of 16 January 1919.

entries.headline: Opening session: Wilson nominates Clemenceau
entries.digest: President Poincaré opened the conference at the French Foreign Ministry on the anniversary of the German Empire's proclamation at Versailles in 1871. Wilson proposed Clemenceau as president of the conference and the nomination was adopted. The real business was already passing to a council of the five great powers' leaders and foreign ministers.
entries.source_note: FRUS, Paris Peace Conference 1919, vol. III, protocol of the first plenary session.

entries.headline: The doctor watches the opening
entries.digest: Grayson accompanied Wilson to the opening and recorded the ceremonial session and the crowd of delegates from many nations in his diary. He was more interested in how the President bore the strain than in the speeches.
entries.source_note: Grayson diary, 18 Jan 1919, as printed in Papers of Woodrow Wilson vol. 54; content summarised in general terms.

entries.headline: Moving that a League be part of the treaty
entries.digest: At the second plenary session Wilson spoke for the resolution that a League of Nations be created as an integral part of the general treaty of peace. The session adopted it and set up a commission, chaired by Wilson, to draft the constitution. Smaller states protested at how few seats they were given on the commissions.
entries.source_note: FRUS, Paris 1919, vol. III, protocol of the plenary session of 25 Jan 1919.

entries.headline: Koo asks for Shandong back
entries.digest: Before the Council of Ten, Koo asked that the leased territory of Kiaochow, the Shandong railway and Germany's other rights in the province be returned directly to China. He argued that the lease had been forced on China, that Shandong was the birthplace of Confucius and part of the nation, and that China's entry into the war had ended Germany's rights. He preferred restitution from Germany, not through Japan.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, Council of Ten, 28 Jan 1919, 11 a.m.

entries.headline: Makino: Japan holds Kiaochow by conquest
entries.digest: Makino answered that Japan had taken Kiaochow from Germany by force and was in actual possession. Japan had undertaken to return the territory to China once it had free disposal of it, and needed Germany's cession first. He referred to agreements already made with China over the railway and offered to share them if Tokyo agreed.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, Council of Ten, 28 Jan 1919.

entries.headline: A memorandum for Arab independence
entries.digest: Faisal submitted a memorandum asking that the Arabic-speaking peoples of Asia be recognised as independent, from a line in the north southward. It set Syria, Iraq and the Hijaz in different stages and left Palestine for separate consideration. He would restate it orally a week later.
entries.source_note: Memorandum of 29 Jan 1919, referred to in FRUS vol. III, Council of Ten, 6 Feb 1919.

entries.headline: Who owns a mandate?
entries.digest: Lansing worked through the legal puzzles of the new mandate system for Germany's former colonies. He asked where sovereignty would lie if neither the inhabitants, the mandatory power nor the League clearly held it, and found no satisfactory answer.
entries.quote: Where does the sovereignty over these territories reside?
entries.source_note: Lansing, The Peace Negotiations (1921), memorandum of 2 Feb 1919.

entries.headline: Faisal before the Council of Ten
entries.digest: Faisal set out the Arab case to the Council of Ten, with Lawrence, Nuri al-Said and Rustum Haidar in attendance. He gave eleven grounds, from shared language to Arab service in the war and Allied promises, and said Syria wanted unity and independence while Lebanon might stand apart. Asked by Wilson whether he wanted one mandatory or several, he said he personally feared partition and proposed an inquiry among the people concerned.
entries.quote: the independence of all the Arabic speaking peoples in Asia
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, Council of Ten (BC-24), 6 Feb 1919, 3 p.m. Quote is from the US secretary's indirect-speech record.

entries.headline: Lawrence at Faisal's shoulder
entries.digest: Lawrence attended the session as a member of the Hijaz delegation, in an army uniform with an Arab headcloth, while British officials including Sir Mark Sykes sat in the same room. The minutes list him as present; later accounts say he put Faisal's Arabic into English. He was serving two masters at once.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, Council of Ten, 6 Feb 1919 (attendance list). The translation detail rests on later accounts.

entries.headline: Interpreting the Arab hearing
entries.digest: Mantoux was listed as interpreter at the Council of Ten when Faisal spoke. French and English were the working languages; the statesmen depended on him to carry argument across the table, and he noted what he heard.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, Council of Ten, 6 Feb 1919 (attendance list).

entries.place: Hôtel Crillon, League of Nations Commission
entries.headline: Proposing equality of nations and their nationals
entries.digest: Makino moved an amendment to the religious-liberty article of the draft Covenant, so that member states would agree to give the nationals of all members equal and just treatment without distinction on account of race or nationality. He reminded the commission that men of different races had fought side by side. The article it was attached to was dropped and the amendment with it.
entries.source_note: Miller, The Drafting of the Covenant; summarised in overviews of the Racial Equality Proposal.

entries.headline: Reading the draft Covenant aloud
entries.digest: Wilson read the twenty-six articles of the draft Covenant to a plenary session and explained them. He presented the League as a flexible body that could grow. That evening he left for Brest to sail home for the end of the congressional session.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, plenary session of 14 Feb 1919. Quote from Wilson's speech in the US record.

entries.headline: No instructions for the treaty
entries.digest: Before Wilson left, Lansing asked him what the commissioners should work on in his absence and suggested subjects for a preliminary treaty. Wilson said he did not care to discuss them then. Lansing recorded it as more evidence that the League came first and the peace second.
entries.source_note: Lansing, The Peace Negotiations (1921), account of 14 Feb 1919.

entries.headline: Left in charge
entries.digest: House noted Wilson's success at the plenary and his departure for the United States, leaving House to represent him on the Council of Ten. House expected to press forward the territorial and military terms while the President was away; the latitude he took would later trouble their friendship.
entries.source_note: House diary, 14 Feb 1919, as excerpted in Seymour, Intimate Papers vol. IV (1928); exact wording not checked.

entries.headline: Off to Brest with the President
entries.digest: Grayson left Paris with the Wilsons on the train to Brest for the voyage home in the George Washington. His diary records the President tired but pleased with the reception of the Covenant.
entries.source_note: Grayson diary, 14–15 Feb 1919, Papers of Woodrow Wilson vol. 55; summarised in general terms.

entries.headline: The Pan-African Congress opens
entries.digest: Diagne opened the first session, praising French colonial policy and hoping that people of African descent everywhere could act together. Du Bois served as secretary. Fifty-seven delegates came from fifteen countries and colonies, the largest groups from the United States, the French West Indies, Haiti and France.
entries.source_note: Du Bois, 'The Pan-African Congress', Cayton's Weekly (Seattle), 19 April 1919.

entries.headline: Resolutions for a League that protects Africans
entries.digest: On its last day the congress adopted resolutions asking that the League of Nations oversee the treatment of Africans in colonies, with rights to land, education and a growing share in government, and that a permanent bureau watch over them. Du Bois reported the results in The Crisis. No delegation of the great powers acted on them.
entries.source_note: The Crisis, April 1919, report on the Pan-African Congress; Library of Congress exhibition. Resolution wording paraphrased from secondary summaries.

entries.headline: The Four begin to meet alone
entries.digest: The heads of government of the United States, Britain, France and Italy began meeting without their foreign ministers, at first with no secretary at all. Mantoux was the only other person in the room, interpreting and taking notes in French that became the fullest record of their talk.
entries.source_note: Mantoux, Les Délibérations du Conseil des Quatre (1955), opening of the notes; Hankey's minutes start later.

entries.headline: The President is suddenly ill
entries.digest: Wilson was taken violently ill in the evening with fever, coughing and diarrhoea during the hardest week of the Council of Four. Grayson treated it as influenza and kept him in bed. House took his place in the Council for several days.
entries.source_note: Grayson diary and his letter to Joseph Tumulty, 3–4 April 1919; Doughboy Foundation summary.

entries.headline: Ordering the ship to Brest
entries.digest: From his sickbed Wilson had Grayson arrange for the George Washington to be sent to Brest, a signal that he was ready to leave if the French did not moderate their demands on the Rhineland and reparations. Grayson saw it as a calculated threat. The ship came; Wilson stayed.
entries.source_note: Grayson diary, 7 April 1919, Papers of Woodrow Wilson vol. 57; date widely reported.

entries.place: Hôtel Crillon, League of Nations Commission
entries.headline: A second try: equality in the preamble
entries.digest: At the commission's final session Makino proposed a more modest text: endorsement of the principle of the equality of nations and just treatment of their nationals, in the Covenant's preamble. He spoke at length about the injury felt in Japan. When Wilson ruled the vote insufficient, the Japanese asked that the minutes record that a majority had supported it.
entries.source_note: Miller, The Drafting of the Covenant; Racial Equality Proposal overview.

entries.headline: Ruling that unanimity is required
entries.digest: Eleven of the seventeen members present voted for the Japanese amendment and none voted against. Wilson, presiding, ruled that because of serious objections a decision of this kind needed unanimity, and the amendment failed. A French delegate pointed out that a majority had voted in favour. The British Empire delegation, pressed by Australia's Hughes, had not supported it.
entries.source_note: League of Nations Commission minutes (Miller, The Drafting of the Covenant).

entries.headline: China votes with Japan on equality
entries.digest: Koo, a member of the commission, supported the Japanese amendment even while China and Japan were locked in dispute over Shandong. Chinese diplomats made clear that for their government Shandong mattered far more.
entries.source_note: League Commission record and later accounts; Koo's individual remarks not checked.

entries.headline: A trip to the devastated areas cancelled
entries.digest: A planned visit to the ruined country near Amiens was given up because of meetings. Stevenson recorded the crisis over Italy's territorial claims under the 1915 Treaty of London and Orlando's position, which was about to bring the Italian delegation's walk-out.
entries.source_note: Frances Stevenson diary, 19 April 1919, in A. J. P. Taylor (ed.), Lloyd George: A Diary (1971).

entries.headline: The Japanese before the Four
entries.digest: Makino and Chinda appeared before the heads of government to press Japan's claim to the German rights in Shandong under its 1917 agreements with Britain and France and its 1915 and 1918 agreements with China. Mantoux's notes record Wilson searching for a formula that would keep Japan in the League without simply handing over the province.
entries.source_note: Mantoux, Délibérations (1955), meeting of 22 April 1919; summarised.

entries.headline: Makino keeps the principle on record
entries.digest: At the plenary that adopted the revised Covenant, Makino stated that Japan would not insist on the equality amendment now but would continue to seek the principle's acceptance. He placed the regret of the Japanese people on the record.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, plenary session of 28 April 1919.

entries.headline: Suspecting a bargain over Shandong
entries.digest: After the plenary Lansing wrote that Japan's quiet acceptance of the Covenant without its equality clause meant a deal had been made: silence on race in exchange for Shandong. He disliked it.
entries.source_note: Lansing, The Peace Negotiations (1921), memorandum of 28 April 1919.

entries.headline: The Three settle Shandong
entries.digest: With Italy absent, Wilson, Lloyd George and Clemenceau agreed that Germany's rights in Shandong would pass to Japan. Japan gave oral assurances that it would return political control to China and keep only economic rights. The record shows Wilson accepting this to keep Japan in the conference and the League.
entries.source_note: Mantoux, Délibérations (1955), meeting of 30 April 1919; FRUS vol. V, Council of Four minutes of the same day.

entries.headline: House for settling with Japan
entries.digest: House had argued that if Japan left the conference the League would be crippled, and favoured a settlement that let Japan take the German rights with promises of return. He recorded relief that the matter was closed, while noting the Chinese would be bitter.
entries.source_note: House diary, late April 1919 (Seymour, Intimate Papers vol. IV); date and wording not checked.

entries.headline: A just but stern peace
entries.digest: Writing home, Stevenson described the treaty as just but stern. She knew Lloyd George had doubts about its severity and that he wanted Germany treated less harshly than the French intended.
entries.source_note: Frances Stevenson's letters from Versailles, National Library of Wales.

entries.headline: 'Returning Soldiers'
entries.digest: Back from France, Du Bois wrote in The Crisis that Black soldiers had fought for a democracy that their own country denied them. He listed lynching, disfranchisement and insult, and said the fight would now continue at home.
entries.quote: We return. We return from fighting. We return fighting.
entries.source_note: The Crisis 18:1 (May 1919), 'Returning Soldiers'.

entries.headline: 'China has been abandoned'
entries.digest: The morning after the decision, Lansing wrote bitterly that the United States had given way to Japan. He doubted the Japanese assurances and thought the settlement betrayed the principles the President had preached.
entries.quote: China has been abandoned to Japanese rapacity.
entries.source_note: Lansing, The Peace Negotiations (1921), memorandum of 1 May 1919.

entries.headline: News from Beijing
entries.digest: On 4 May about three thousand students marched in Beijing against the Shandong decision and burned the house of a minister they blamed for the secret agreements with Japan. Over the following weeks the delegation in Paris was flooded with telegrams from students, merchants and provincial groups urging it not to sign. Koo later remembered the pressure as decisive.
entries.source_note: Koo, oral-history memoir (recorded 1960s–70s). The May Fourth demonstration itself is well documented.

entries.headline: Receiving the terms, answering seated
entries.digest: Clemenceau told the Germans there would be no oral discussion: they had fifteen days to reply in writing. Brockdorff-Rantzau answered in a long statement in German, translated sentence by sentence; observers noted that he stayed seated. He refused the charge that Germany alone was guilty, admitted the wrong done to Belgium, asked for an impartial inquiry and held the Allies to Wilson's principles.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, protocol of the session of 7 May 1919 at the Trianon Palace. His remaining seated is from press and eyewitness reports.

entries.headline: A cold meeting at the Trianon
entries.digest: Grayson went with Wilson to the Trianon and described the Germans' entry and the speech in his diary. He reported that the Allied leaders took Brockdorff-Rantzau's manner as defiance.
entries.source_note: Grayson diary, 7 May 1919, Papers of Woodrow Wilson vol. 58; summarised in general terms.

entries.headline: The terms read in full
entries.digest: The day after the terms were delivered, Lansing set down his impression of the finished treaty: disappointment and depression. He judged the terms harsh enough to create grievances and thought the League built into them would not hold back another war.
entries.quote: The terms of peace appear immeasurably harsh and humiliating
entries.source_note: Lansing, The Peace Negotiations (1921), memorandum of 8 May 1919.

entries.headline: Asia Minor divided over a map
entries.digest: Nicolson was called to Lloyd George's flat, where Wilson, Lloyd George and Clemenceau stood over a large map of Asia Minor deciding zones for Italy and Greece. He was appalled at the speed and ignorance with which the fates of whole populations were being settled.
entries.source_note: Nicolson, Peacemaking 1919 (1933), diary for 13 May 1919. Not quoted (post-1928 publication).

entries.headline: The German counter-proposals
entries.digest: The German delegation delivered its written observations on the draft treaty. It offered large reparations and disarmament on conditions but rejected the war-guilt article, the loss of territory in the east and the exclusion from the League, and appealed again to the Fourteen Points.
entries.source_note: German observations on the conditions of peace, 29 May 1919 (printed in FRUS vol. VI).

entries.headline: Waiting for the signature
entries.digest: After dining with a general posted in Berlin, Stevenson wrote that the delay was dangerous: Germany was unsettled and nothing could move until people knew the peace was signed. Lloyd George was pushing the Council to soften some terms.
entries.source_note: Frances Stevenson's letters from Versailles (early June 1919), National Library of Wales.

entries.headline: An acknowledgment, nothing more
entries.digest: The petition was acknowledged by the American delegation and filed. It was never discussed by the Council. The demands circulated among Vietnamese in France and in the left-wing press.
entries.source_note: US National Archives RG 256 file; standard biographies. Exact dates of replies not checked.

entries.headline: Eight demands for the Annamite people
entries.digest: Nguyen Ai Quoc sent Lansing a short covering letter with the 'Claims of the Annamite People', asking the conference to support eight reforms: political amnesty, equal justice, freedom of the press, association, travel and education, rule by law instead of decree, and elected Vietnamese representatives in the French parliament. Copies went to other delegations.
entries.source_note: Letter of 18 June 1919 with enclosure, US National Archives RG 256, 851G.00 (NAID 5049414), on DocsTeach.

entries.headline: Resigning rather than sign
entries.digest: When the Allies rejected most German objections and gave a deadline, Brockdorff-Rantzau advised the cabinet to refuse. The Scheidemann government resigned on 20 June and he left office with it. A new government accepted the treaty under protest three days later.
entries.source_note: Standard histories of the Weimar Republic; dates of the cabinet fall and the 23 June vote.

entries.headline: The treaty is signed
entries.digest: In the Hall of Mirrors, where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871, the German delegates Hermann Müller and Johannes Bell signed first, followed by the Allied plenipotentiaries. The ceremony fell on the fifth anniversary of the Sarajevo assassination. Wilson left Paris for Brest by train that evening.
entries.source_note: FRUS vol. III, protocol of the session of 28 June 1919; Orpen painting (IWM).

entries.headline: Empty Chinese chairs
entries.digest: The Chinese delegation, refused permission to sign with a reservation on Shandong, stayed away and issued a statement explaining why. Koo later remembered being driven through Paris that day, feeling it was a dark day for China.
entries.source_note: Koo, oral-history memoir (dictated decades later); the Chinese delegation's absence is in the official record.

entries.headline: A spectator at the signing
entries.digest: Nicolson described the hall packed with guests, the two German delegates led in pale and silent, the signatures and the guns firing outside, and the crowd's eagerness to get autographs. He went to bed that night disgusted with the whole business.
entries.source_note: Nicolson, Peacemaking 1919 (1933), diary for 28 June 1919. Not quoted.

entries.headline: Parting advice to the President
entries.digest: Before Wilson left, House urged him to meet the Senate in a conciliatory spirit, as he had his foreign colleagues. Wilson answered that nothing worth having in life was won without a fight. House recorded the exchange; it was the last time they met.
entries.source_note: House diary, 28 June 1919, quoted in American Heritage, 'Epilogue'.

entries.headline: Looking back on eight months
entries.digest: House wrote a reflective entry on leaving Paris with mixed feelings. He thought the conference might have chosen a new path and had not, but argued that the treaty and the League were better than the alternatives.
entries.source_note: House diary, end of June 1919, Seymour, Intimate Papers vol. IV (1928); exact day (28 or 29 June) not checked.

convergences.label: The opening session at the Quai d'Orsay
convergences.note: The official protocol records a ceremony; Grayson watches the President's stamina; Lansing, two days earlier, had already written that the Americans had no plan.

convergences.label: Shandong heard by the Council of Ten
convergences.note: The same territory argued from law and nationality by Koo and from conquest and treaty by Makino, in the same room and in the same minutes.

convergences.label: Faisal before the Council of Ten
convergences.note: The Arab case as Faisal put it, the British officer beside him, the interpreter carrying it across, and Wilson's question about one mandatory or several.

convergences.label: The draft Covenant read; Wilson sails
convergences.note: Wilson's triumph in the plenary, Lansing's unanswered request for instructions, House left in charge, and Grayson on the train to Brest.

convergences.label: The racial-equality vote
convergences.note: A majority with no votes against, a chairman's ruling, and the Chinese delegate supporting his rival's principle while the two fought over Shandong.

convergences.label: Shandong settled
convergences.note: Decided by three men in Wilson's study; House relieved, Lansing furious the next morning, and within days students marching in Beijing.

convergences.label: Terms handed to the Germans at the Trianon
convergences.note: The defeated foreign minister's answer, the Americans' reading of his manner, and Lansing's private verdict on the terms written the next day.

convergences.label: Signing in the Hall of Mirrors; China absent
convergences.note: The official ceremony, a weary diplomat's disgust, a last conversation between friends, and China's empty chairs.

ties.note: Closest of collaborators in January; after Wilson's return in March the friendship cooled, and their parting on 28 June 1919 was their last meeting.
Secretary of State and President in the same delegation; Lansing's dated notes record disagreement on the League, on secrecy and on Shandong. Wilson dismissed him in 1920.
Rival claimants to Shandong before the Council of Ten on 28 January, yet on the same side of the racial-equality vote on 11 April.
Lawrence had served with Faisal in the Arab revolt and came to Paris as his adviser; he translated Faisal's reservation to the Weizmann agreement.
Mantoux interpreted for Wilson in the Council of Four and wrote the notes through which Wilson's words in that room are known.
Interpreter at the Council of Ten session of 6 February when Faisal presented the Arab case.
The petition of 18 June was addressed to Lansing; it survives in the American delegation's files.
Brockdorff-Rantzau's speech and notes appealed repeatedly to Wilson's own principles against the terms Wilson had helped write.
Physician and daily companion; Grayson's diary records Wilson's illness of April 1919 and every journey.
Nicolson's 13 May scene over the map of Asia Minor took place at Lloyd George's flat in the rue Nitot, where Stevenson worked.
Lansing's memoranda of 28 April and 1 May sided with China's claim; he later told the Senate he had yielded only out of duty to the President.
House and the Japanese delegates negotiated wordings for the equality clause in February and March before the April vote.
Du Bois came to Paris hoping to bring Africa's case to the President and the conference; the Pan-African Congress met with no great-power delegation present.

threads_out.note: The conference was the war's settlement. Harry Graf Kessler, a diarist in the First World War chapter, recorded the German reaction to the terms in Berlin in May and June 1919.

Du Bois, an eye in the Harlem chapter, convened the Pan-African Congress two days after the 369th Infantry, the 'Harlem Hellfighters', paraded up Fifth Avenue to Harlem on 17 February 1919. His 'Returning Soldiers' editorial of May 1919 joined the two causes.
Paris was planned in the shadow of the last great European congress: the British Foreign Office commissioned Charles Webster's study of the Congress of Vienna as a handbook for its 1919 delegation.

Franklin Roosevelt, then Assistant Secretary of the Navy, was in Paris in early 1919 and sailed home with Wilson on the George Washington in February; at Yalta he worked to build the United Nations on the lessons of the League.

The petitioner turned away in 1919 led the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, which sent a delegation to Bandung in 1955; China, which refused to sign at Versailles, sent Zhou Enlai. Racial equality, rejected in Paris, was a founding theme there.
